claims.text: The coatings are high-entropy-alloy multilayers fabricated by sputter deposition.
The coatings exhibit distinct compositional layers.
The compositional layers have well-defined interfaces.
Changing deposition parameters can produce interfaces with different degrees of chemical disorder and structural coherency.
The degree of chemical disorder and structural incoherency at multilayer interfaces governs resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Chemically disordered, incoherent interfaces act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Chemically disordered, incoherent interfaces act as barriers to dislocation climb.
Incoherent interfaces create mismatches in local atomic order.
Incoherent interfaces create mismatches in local mechanical properties.
The local mismatches increase the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Increasing barriers to dislocation glide and climb slows time-dependent plastic deformation.
At identical stress and temperature, coatings with highly disordered, incoherent interfaces will have lower creep rates than coatings with more coherent interfaces.
At identical stress and temperature, coatings with highly disordered, incoherent interfaces will have lower creep rates than homogeneous HEA coatings.
The interface-mediated effect will be most pronounced at moderate-to-high temperatures where thermal activation assists dislocation climb.
The interface-mediated effect will be most pronounced for nanoscale layer thicknesses.
At very low temperatures, the interface-mediated effect may be less significant.
For layer thicknesses beyond the nanoscale regime, the interface-mediated effect may be less significant.
High-resolution TEM can distinguish interface coherency and chemical disorder between the comparison groups.
